title: Why Private Markets Need Modern Infrastructure
excerpt: Private market infrastructure helps Canadian property owners reach dealers whose clients want private real estate, with consistent diligence and clear records.

children.text: Few investors think about how a stock exchange routes their order. The systems behind public markets are familiar enough that investors can leave the details to others. In private markets, even routine changes can take more work. Somewhere, a car is finding its way through traffic without a driver, yet getting a verified banking change into a payment record can still depend on people exchanging emails and updating spreadsheets by hand.

The appetite for private investments is there. For investors, access can depend on what their dealer can offer. For dealers, assessing an offering requires reliable information. Once an investment is made, administrators need to keep ownership records and payment details current as circumstances change.

Ocree is building infrastructure for commercial real estate. It helps property owners reach dealers whose clients are looking for private investments. A consistent package of documents gives dealers the information they need to review an offering within the rules that govern how it can be offered.
Traditional and Digital Finance Are Converging

In Project Samara, Export Development Canada issued a digital bond to a closed group of investors. RBC Capital Markets and TD Securities were the joint lead managers. The Bank of Canada issued the wholesale central bank money used to settle the transaction.
The experiment worked technically, according to the Bank of Canada's research paper. It identified potential benefits for data integrity and reductions in counterparty and settlement risk.

In its 2025 Annual Economic Report, the Bank for International Settlements explained how tokenization could combine transaction information and asset transfers in one process. That helps explain the interest in this infrastructure. Records and transfers that are handled separately today could be managed together.
Ocree is hearing a change in dealers' questions, too. They are asking less about how the technology works and more about the problems it can solve.
I think it's more so combining the two worlds, Ted Davis, Ocree's co-founder and CEO, said at Tokenize North in Montreal in September 2026.
Access Is the Product

An individual may want to invest in private real estate and still struggle to find an offering. What they can invest in depends partly on eligibility rules in their province. Their dealer also needs enough information to assess the offering.

The driver is being able to access products that are difficult to access today, Davis says. Buying a listed stock has a familiar starting point. With private real estate, a client may be interested but unsure where to find an offering their dealer supports. They may also assume these investments are closed to them.

Deloitte's Center for Financial Services projects that global tokenized real estate could reach US$ 4 trillion by 2035, up from less than US$ 300 billion in 2024. Its forecast covers a range of real estate interests and financing structures. That is a projection of adoption rather than investment performance. For dealers, it gives scale to a practical question about how investors will find and evaluate these offerings.

In Canada, most securities are sold with a prospectus. Private real estate offerings usually rely on exemptions from that requirement instead. Accredited investor status is the most commonly known exemption. Others exist, though their availability depends on the offering, the investor and the province or territory. Each comes with its own conditions, which can include limits on how much an individual may invest.

Qualifying under an exemption does not mean an investment is suitable. Exempt market investments can be hard to sell, may come with less ongoing disclosure, and can lose some or all of their value. A registered dealer assesses suitability before a client invests.
Private Market Infrastructure That Works Inside the Existing System

Private real estate already runs on established relationships. Property owners bring offerings to dealers, who review them for their clients. Ocree's approach gives these firms shared digital infrastructure to work from. An offering could then reach more dealers without each firm having to start from scratch.

If you want true scale, it's the integration, says Davis. Putting an offering into a digital format is only part of the work. It still needs to reach the firms that serve investors. A separate marketplace would still need those connections.

Ocree's Asset Rating & Disclosure System, or OARDS, brings commercial real estate due diligence and valuation information into a standard format. This gives dealers a consistent set of information to work from when conducting their own review.

As dealers join and their systems connect, investors could find offerings through firms they already use. Ocree is currently participating in an industry pilot to test connections between existing market participants.
What Each Participant Gains
Each participant in a private real estate transaction meets a different kind of friction. Modern infrastructure is designed to reduce it for all three at once.

children.text: Consider an illustrative transfer. A client in Oakville transfers half her units in a Mississauga industrial property to her daughter's holding company, effective March 27. Assume the offering bases distributions on ownership as of March 31. The payment file still comes from last month's spreadsheet. The client receives the full distribution while her daughter's company receives nothing.

The paperwork was complete. The payment process simply hadn't caught up. A shared ownership record that updates once an authorized transfer is approved could let the administrator apply the change under the offering's terms.

The history matters too. If an issuer changes administrators, the incoming firm needs to account for every holding it inherits. A ledger can preserve the sequence of ownership changes. Linked approval records can show the authority behind each one, provided that history stays accessible when providers change.
Why the Combination of Expertise Matters

Davis describes the model as a three-legged stool. Technology is the first leg. Understanding the product, from sourcing an asset to what investors need, is the second. A compliance-first relationship with regulators is the third. An existing market does not need to be proven. What needs to be proven is a better way to distribute it. Ocree brings those disciplines together to modernize how private market investments reach investors.
